articles.title: Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
articles.summary: The government blames overcrowding, poor maintenance, and missing life jackets for boat accidents.

blocks.text: Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.

"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.

In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

The two Americans convicted of murdering Quebec entrepreneur Daniel Langlois and his partner Dominique Marchand in Dominica in December 2023 were sentenced on Monday to life in prison without parole.

The two Americans convicted of murdering Quebec entrepreneur Daniel Langlois and his partner Dominique Marchand in Dominica have been sentenced to life in prison without parole.
Jonathan Lehrer and Robert Thomas Snyder Jr. were found guilty in July of killing the couple in December 2023.
The victims' bodies were discovered in a burned-out vehicle near a luxury eco-resort they owned on the island.
Prosecutor Keith Scotland says the Americans have appealed the verdict and can also appeal the sentence.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Marcos confronted Romualdez over insertions that would have laid off 7,000 DPWH staff --Bonoan
articles.summary: Pres. Marcos Jr. confronted then-House Speaker Romualdez over the near-layoff of some 7,000 daily wage employees of the DPWH due to congressional insertions in 2024, Manuel Bonoan said.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 8:01pm

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. confronted then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez over the near-layoff of some 7,000 daily wage employees of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) due to congressional insertions in 2024, former DPWH secretary Manuel Bonoan stated in a judicial affidavit exclusively obtained by GMA News.

Bonoan said the DPWH was cash-strapped after legislators took the budget allotted for its Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) to allocate it to more than 9,000 congressional insertions worth P 380.48 billion.
Legislators also took the more than P70.701 billion allocated for infrastructure projects or foreign-assisted projects like the Metro Manila Subway Project or the North South Rail Commuter Project.
“… the legislators took everything leaving nothing for the IFP/FAP,” Bonoan said.
Bonoan said the President immediately called Romualdez after he had informed him about this.

“The President was so concerned about laying off 7,000 DPWH daily wage employees, so he immediately called [then-] Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez in my presence. To my recollection, the President told Speaker Martin, ‘Ano ba naman kayo, magtatanggal si Secretary Manny ng 7,000 employees dahil kinuha n’yo pati MOOE n’ya. Hindi pwede ito,” he said.
Bonoan said Romualdez reprimanded him for reporting to the President..
“Sometime after that Speaker Martin Romualdez called me up and told me ‘Pambihira ka naman Sec., pwede ka namang dumeretso sa akin, nagsumbong ka pa kay Presidente,” Bonoan recounted.
Bonoan told Romualdez that the President was his boss.
But despite the President’s warning, it continued even in the 2025 budget.

“Notwithstanding the phone call of the President, the House Of Representatives and the Senate of the Philippines still slashed the Department’s proposed budget for the Fiscal Year 2025 to fund their ‘congressional initiatives’ or ‘insertions,” Bonoan said.
In 2025, there was some P436 billion in congressional insertions according to Bonoan which irked the President that he wanted to veto the whole 2025 budget.
“The President was furious that he wanted to veto the entire 2025 GAB but his economic managers advised the President not to,” Bonoan said.

The President then instructed Bonoan to identify which projects he could veto and Bonoan identified some P26 billion pesos of infrastructure projects which he called “guni-guni” projects that included highways in mountains that run to legislators’ resorts.

“These projects I recommended to be vetoed are ambiguous or ‘guni-guni’ projects that I reported to the President. These projects were construction of highways to the mountains leading to resorts of legislators, construction of new buildings, hostels and swimming pools, etc. These projects are not aligned with the core programs of the government,” Bonoan said.

Of the P400 billion in insertions, P192 billion came from the House of Representatives while some P17 billion were “jointly tagged under the names of both senators and members of the House of Representatives.”
Bonoan furnished the court with a listing of Romualdez alleged insertions including that of former House Committee on Appropriations Chair Zaldy Co.
A GMA News source said Romualdez’ amount of insertions is around P27 billion.
GMA News sought the Romualdez and Co’s comments but their counsels refused comment. — BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war

blocks.text: Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in

blocks.text: Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

blocks.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

articles.title: Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
articles.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.

blocks.text: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

articles.title: Presidential villa also hit by water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
articles.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - failures that plague ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

articles.title: Democrats reveal details for 2028 presidential primary following midterm victories – US politics live
articles.summary: Party says there will be 12 debates to select a candidate from what is expected to be a large number of hopefuls

blocks.text: Democrats plan 12 debates for 2028 presidential primary
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Democrats are planning 12 presidential primary debates for what’s expected to be a crowded field of 2028 candidates, with the first scheduled for June, the Democratic National Committee has said.

The DNC’s announcement on Monday comes before major candidates have launched campaigns to succeed term-limited Republican president Donald Trump and follows the party’s convincing midterm performance, AP reported.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement the party is aimed at staying united and helping the eventual nominee win the White House. “The DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” he said.
Anticipating a large number of presidential hopefuls, the DNC said it will cap participation in each debate to 20 qualifying candidates over two nights, if needed.

The criteria for making the debate stage will be similar to 2020, when there was also a big field and a dozen debates, the DNC said, and will include meeting polling and other criteria such as grassroots fundraising.

More details are set to be announced in January, including specific times and locations for the debates, the DNC said, though the party confirmed that five debates will be in 2027 and seven in 2028. The final primary debate is planned for March 2028.

For the first time, candidates must pledge to reject dark money as a condition of making the debate stage. The new requirement is part of a ​DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.

The debate schedule is one of the most closely watched decisions the DNC makes, along with selecting the city for the 2028 convention. Earlier this year, the DNC narrowed the list of cities to Boston, Denver and Philadelphia.

blocks.text: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
Ramon Antonio Vargas
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage. “If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China. Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”. The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday.

Democrats have won their largest majority in the House in more than three decades after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina on Sunday, extending the blue wave that swept the US midterms and increasing pressure on the party to deliver its promises to US voters. House Democrats have secured at least 258 seats in a midterm election sweep unseen since 1992, gaining 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.

articles.title: SC: Child remains legitimate even if father is unnamed in birth certificate
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child"s birth certificate.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 7:06pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child’s birth certificate.

In a nine-page resolution, the SC Third Division granted a woman’s petition to correct her birth certificate to reflect her proper middle name and surname, as well as the date of her parents’ marriage.

“Under Article 164 of the Family Code, ‘children conceived or born during the marriage are legitimate.’ This means that legitimacy as a status attaches once a person is born within wedlock,” the Court said.

The petitioner’s parents were legally married when she was born. However, her mother registered her birth under her maiden surname, used her own middle name for her daughter and left the father’s identity blank because the couple were not on good terms at the time.
The High Court said Article 167 of the Family Code provides that a child remains legitimate even if the mother declares otherwise, including in the child’s birth certificate.
The petitioner grew up using her father’s surname in her school and employment records, including her Professional Regulation Commission identification card.
She discovered the discrepancies in her birth certificate only in 2017, prompting her to seek its correction.

The SC said substantial corrections to civil registry records may be sought under Rule 108 of the Rules of Court through adversarial proceedings, in which interested parties are notified and given the opportunity to contest the requested changes.
In her concurring opinion, Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh also cited Rule 108, saying it may be used to correct entries in civil records that affect a person's legitimacy or filiation.

“A petition under Rule 108 is a procedural device to cancel or correct entries in the civil register, including entries relating to birth and filiation, subject to due process requirements,” Singh wrote.

She cited Section 2 of Rule 108, which allows the cancellation or correction of civil registry entries on valid grounds, including births, marriages, deaths, legitimations, adoptions, acknowledgments of natural children, judicial determinations of filiation and changes of name.

The Court ordered the concerned local civil registrar to amend the petitioner's birth certificate by replacing her middle name with her mother's maiden surname, changing her last name to her father's surname and indicating the date of her parents' marriage.
The resolution was penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao and promulgated on April 7, 2026.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
articles.summary: Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of…

image.caption: Police responded to bomb threats against multiple schools but were working on the preliminary assumption they were hoaxesImage: Carsten Rehder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in several locations across Germany are reporting large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They say that while they are investigating the claims, they do not currently have reason to treat them as credible threats. Police in Erfurt and Freiburg were among the first to report the phenomenon on Monday.
What did police say about the bomb threats?

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."
Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.
Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.
Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.
As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."
Various disruptive incidents targeting Europe in recent weeks
This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Europe.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.
This is a developing story, more to follow...

articles.title: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
articles.summary:
Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped

The

blocks.text: The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.
But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.
“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.
Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.

The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.
An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

articles.title: This B.C. man found some historical parkas at a thrift store — now he's trying to get them back to Nunavut
articles.summary: Mike Williams of Kamloops discovered that the parkas were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Alaska. He's determined to get them back to the northern community where they…

image.caption: Mike Williams, left, of Kamloops, B.C., shows CBC reporter Doug Herbert some hand-made parkas he recently found at a thrift store in his city. Williams has since found out they were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, more than 50 years ago, and he wants to see them go back to the community. (Peter Cameron-I

blocks.text: North

Mike Williams of Kamloops discovered that the parkas were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Alaska. He's determined to get them back to the northern community where they were made.
Mike Williams found 4 hand-made parkas from Taloyoak, Nunavut
Selena ‘Kublu’ Tucktoo of Taloyoak, Nunavut, remembers making parkas with her mom back when Tucktoo was in her early 20s.
“It was kind of complicated at first, but I learned,” she said. “They were fun to do. Lots of sewing.”

Tucktoo said she and other seamstresses in her community were making the parkas for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games happening in Anchorage, Alaska. Once the garments headed to the event, she didn’t expect to see them again.
Until now.
Selena 'Kublu' Tucktoo of Taloyoak was surprised to learn that a parka she created for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games was among those found at the Kamloops thrift store. (Liny Lamberink/CBC)
Some of those parkas were recently found at a thrift store in Kamloops, B.C. — and could soon be heading back to where they came from.

Mike Williams, a retired IT worker in Kamloops, found a parka bearing Tucktoo’s name at a Value Village in his city in mid-October, along with three others of a similar style. They caught his eye, but he didn’t buy them right away.
“I think it was the next day I went in, and they were still there, and I took a closer look at them and I knew they were special. So I bought them,” he recalled.
Williams bought the 4 parkas in mid-October, originally thinking he'd re-sell them. But as he learned more about their history, he decided to do something else. (Submitted by Mike Williams)
At the time, Williams thought he might be able to make money re-selling the parkas. They’d cost him $325 altogether.
But he was curious about them, so he posted about his find on social media and soon was in touch with people who knew more about the garments. That's when he realized he didn't want to sell them.
“I think they were meant to return to the community, and I think I was meant to get them there,” he said.
Hundreds of outfits made by craft collective

Arnaqarvik was a craft collective that started in the early 1970s in Taloyoak, then known as Spence Bay. Judy McGrath, who moved there from Newfoundland, and Arnaoyok Alookee, of Taloyoak, were instrumental in getting it off the ground, according to the Kitikmeot Heritage Society.
The society says the collective was contracted to design and produce nearly 400 outfits for athletes and dignitaries from the Northwest Territories for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games.
Archival photos show the parkas being worn by flag-bearers marching at the event in Alaska.

A photo in the N.W.T. Archives shows flag-bearers marching at the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Anchorage, Alaska. (NWT Archives/Northwest Territories. Department of Public Works and Services fonds/G-1995-001: 0819)

In an email to CBC News, a collections manager with the Kitikmeot Heritage Society in Nunavut said the four parkas Williams found seem consistent in their materials and manufacturing, and pointed out that some have a “WG,” which stands for "Winter Games," on their labels.

Three of the parkas Williams found still have labels attached bearing the names of the people who made them. The fourth, an amauti-style parka designed to carry a baby in the hood, has the name of its steamstress embroidered in Inuktitut syllabics.

Three of the parkas Williams found have labels attached to them with the name of the seamstress who made them. The seamstress who made the an amauti-style parka designed to carry a baby in the hood, is identifiable by a name embroidered in Inuktitut syllabics. (Mike Williams)
Tucktoo was surprised when she heard about Williams's find at the Kamloops thrift store, and curious about how they ended up there.
“How come the people that wore them didn’t keep them, I wonder?” she said, speaking to CBC News on Tuesday during a visit to Yellowknife. “Maybe it’s not their style? I don’t know.”
Getting them back to Taloyoak
Williams was eventually able to get in contact with people in Taloyoak about the parkas, including some living family members of seamstresses who’ve since died.
He's now trying to figure out the best way to get the garments back home.
A photo of the parka designs that the Arnaqarvik collective created for the Arctic Winter Games in 1974. (Kitikmeot Heritage Society)
Worried that a parcel might get lost somewhere along the 2,500-kilometre journey, Williams started thinking about delivering the parkas himself.

He was initially discouraged when he looked up the cost of flights. A return flight between Edmonton and Taloyoak in early December would cost more than $3,000, so he decided to reach out to airlines and ask for help.
Canadian North responded, and offered Williams and his wife free flights to the community.
The challenge now, however, is finding accommodation when they get to the community of around 1,000 people. But Williams said he’s determined to get the parkas back to Taloyoak, one way or another.
What happens to the parkas after that has not yet been decided. One idea that’s emerged from speaking with community members, Williams said, is to put the parkas on display at Taloyoak’s high school.

items: Repatriation of Indigenous artifacts key for cultural identity: Northern leaders
A Tlingit artist is on a mission to return a traditional artifact to its original home

blocks.text: Pangniq High School principal Rod Drover told CBC News on Thursday he was just learning of the garments — but he was enthusiastic about making them part of a display the school is working on in its foyer. He encouraged Williams to get in touch with him.
"This is exciting stuff," Drover said.
“Our desire is to celebrate the culture, making sure we have artifacts, things of history, relevance, and to showcase it, not only to our students but to the community.”
Williams said he’d bring the garments to the school and let the community decide from there what to do with them.
"They know what's best," he said.
Tucktoo supports having the parkas put on display somewhere in Taloyoak, but she’s also interested in having the one she made returned to her directly.
“I’m sure my daughter would love to use it for patterns.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Liny Lamberink is a reporter for CBC North, covering the Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon. She moved to Yellowknife in March 2021, after working as a reporter and newscaster in Ontario for five years. You can reach her at liny.lamberink@cbc.ca

articles.title: 'I've Lost Her Forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
articles.summary: For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or…

image.caption: Because she won't sign a new contract with an AI clause, Katrin Fröhlich will no longer be the German voice of Cameron Diaz on NetflixImage: Netflix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.
For over 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.
But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.
Netflix contract sparks AI dispute

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.
The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.
They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

blocks.caption: Katrin Fröhlich, who has dubbed the German voice of Cameron Diaz for over 30 years, is worried about the future of the voiceover industryImage: Nicole Kubelka/Geisler-Fotopress/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."
"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.
Union says deal offers legal safeguards
The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.
Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.
"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.
Is AI killing creative jobs?

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.
"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."
He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.
Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.
"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

blocks.caption: Matti Klemm is the voice of children's character Benjamin BlümchenImage: RTL+/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voice actor plans legal challenge
Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon character Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."
He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.
The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

blocks.caption: Matti Klemm wants to find out exactly how Netflix has used his voice to train its AI and is suing the companyImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"
Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.
Industry fears growing AI impact

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.
Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.
"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.
Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.
"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.
But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

articles.title: Senate begins plenary deliberations for 2027 national budget
articles.summary: Senators are proposing P204.634 billion in amendments in the 2027 national budget

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate on Monday, November 23, began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, with lawmakers proposing P204.634 billion in amendments that prioritize “basic needs,” including health care and education, while cutting billions of pesos in infrastructure projects.

Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate finance committee, sponsored Committee Report No. 131 on House Bill No. 10858, or the General Appropriations Bill (GAB), formally bringing the proposed budget to the plenary for deliberations.
In his sponsorship speech, Ejercito bat for a “back to basics” approach in the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget, emphasizing the need to prioritize essential services.

“Health care, food security, education, livelihood, employment, and security — these are the things that we want to focus on during our outlining and deliberations of the 2027 national budget. Back to basics,” Ejercito said.
“Before we focus on complicated matters, we should focus what limited resources we have on ensuring that the basic needs of our people are provided,” he said.
The Senate’s P204.634-billion proposed amendments include a P97-billion reduction in the allocation for 3,463 projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

These include 36 DPWH buildings, 295 projects deemed noncompliant for lacking proper documentation under the National Expenditure Program, and 3,132 noncompliant projects that appeared only in the House-approved GAB.
Ejercito previously said the reductions in the DPWH budget would be realigned to foreign-assisted infrastructure projects, which saw a P130-billion decrease in the House-approved GAB.

Budget watchdogs People’s Budget Coalition and BetterGovPH had earlier flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion that lacked published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget. PBC also tracked some 6,200 DPWH projects worth P170 million that were inserted into the budget.
“This, Mr. President, is the direction we want to pursue in the 2027 national budget. Back to basics, but with a clear vision for economic recovery and nation-building,” said Ejercito.
Under the Senate version of the budget, the health sector received a P52-billion increase, with funding partly sourced from realignments within the Department of Health (DOH).

State health insurer Philippine Health Insurance Corporation, or PhilHealth, received an additional P19.8 billion, raising its allocation from P74.4 billion under the House-approved GAB to P94.2 billion in the Senate version.

The DOH Office of the Secretary received an additional P9.6 billion, increasing its budget to P378.6 billion. This includes P5.49 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, P1.09 billion for health promotion programs, P1.5 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu transition.
The Senate realigned funding for medical assistance to the Zero Balance Billing program, allocating P1 billion for local government-run hospitals.

The education sector, meanwhile, received P915.4 billion in the Senate’s budget bill. Of this amount, P11.8 billion will go to the Department of Education, including P11 billion for the School-Based Feeding Program to support the universal feeding program for kindergarten to Grade 1 students.

State universities and colleges will receive P138.2 billion for the continued construction and improvement of their school buildings, with each SUC receiving P7.5 million for the Smart Campus Project — a program that would provide internet connectivity to over 100 campuses.
The Senate budget bill also provides additional P33.1 billion in funding for foreign-assisted infrastructure projects, primarily to restore funding cuts in the House-approved GAB.
Among these are P4.7 billion to restore the government’s counterpart funding for the Metro Manila Subway Project and P15 billion in loan proceeds for the North-South Commuter Railway project.
A combined P146.5 million will also be allocated for the NCR Busway Project, Active Transport Bike Share System, and Safe Pathways Program.
The Senate also allocated budget to enhance food security and ensure productivity of farmlands amid the threat of Super El Niño, earmarking P251 billion for the Department of Agriculture (DA).

This includes an additional P4 billion for the DA’s Rice Program to help boost rice production; a P250 million fund for programs helping farmers amid the impending drought; and an augmentation of P1 billion for the DA’s Quick Response Fund to “assist our farmers the earliest time the streams and wells show signs of drying up.”

More than P1 billion was allotted for the establishment of the storage facility Benguet AgriPinoy Trading Center, while P50 million and P200 million were allocated for the construction of a cold storage facility in Barlig, Mountain Province and Oriental Mindoro, respectively.
The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development will also receive P4.04 billion to support the Expanded Pambansang Pabahay para sa Pilipino Program.

Meanwhile, senators provided an additional P1.73 billion to the Department of National Defense, hiking its budget to P326.9 billion. This is on top of the P50 billion earmarked for the continued modernization of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

Ejercito also underscored the need to strengthen the capabilities of the Philippine Navy to improve maritime patrols and reinforce the country’s presence in the West Philippine Sea. The Philippine Coast Guard, for its part, will receive P45.6 billion, including an additional P146.8-million allocation, to support its operations and maritime security efforts.

Ejercito filed the committee report on November 20. It was signed by 18 senators, including senators Tito Sotto, Migz Zubiri, Bam Aquino, Bong Go, Risa Hontiveros, Kiko Pangilinan, Erwin Tulfo, Joel Villanueva, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Lito Lapid, Raffy Tulfo, Imee Marcos, Robinhood Padilla, Mark Villar, Pia Cayetano, and Camille Villar.
In a manifestation, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano explained why he did not sign the committee report.

“My signature is not on that committee report not because I did not want to sign but because it is physically impossible to come up with a good judgment, even if I do trust the chairman of the committee on finance, Senator JV,” Cayetano said.
Senators are working on a tight schedule to ratify the budget bill and avoid a reenacted budget in 2027.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said over the weekend that the country could not afford another reenacted budget, arguing that a fresh spending plan would help stimulate the economy.

“If we have a new budget, we will have new spending, because if we analyze it, one of our country’s economic problems is slow spending. So, the 2027 budget will serve as a stimulus program to it,” Gatchalian told DZBB Super Radyo.
The Senate is eyeing holding an open bicameral conference committee on the proposed 2027 budget on December 13, with ratification targeted for December 17.

Apart from the budget, the Commission on Appointments (CA) is also racing against time to process the appointments of at least 35 presidential appointees, including Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, and military officers, before its December 17 adjournment.
Gatchalian said the CA would hold three hearings before the break, from 8 am to 12 pm, ahead of the Senate’s plenary budget deliberations at 1 pm.
Senators are hoping to conclude the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before the end of the year. The trial is currently on a brief break and is scheduled to resume on December 1.
“Whatever the ruling is — be it conviction or acquittal — the consensus is we want to finish the trial before end of the year,” Gatchalian added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism
articles.summary: Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.

image.caption: Demonstrations against the far-right AfD have drawn thousands of participantsImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

The "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.

"In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.
Politically-disillusioned youth? Far from it!
Lasting damage to democracy in Germany?
According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.
The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.

The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.

But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, CLAIM.

The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.
Games with purpose — more than entertainment
AfD: 'Program to secure power by the Left'
The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."

If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.
In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."

However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.
German influencer fights extremism on TikTok
How is democratic civil society prioritized?
"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."

Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.

"The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she said.

For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.
The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Samchan exec's testimony crucial to Romualdez plunder case -- Ombudsman spox
articles.summary: The testimony of Felicito Guevarra, an executive of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., could prove crucial to the Ombudsman's P7.4-billion plunder case against former House Speaker Martin Romualdez and…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 6:38pm

The testimony of Felicito Guevarra, an executive of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., could prove crucial to the Ombudsman's P7.4-billion plunder case against former House Speaker Martin Romualdez and his co-accused, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said on Monday.

Clavano made the statement after the Ombudsman asked the Sandiganbayan to discharge Guevarra as a co-accused so he could act as a prosecution witness in Romualdez's bail hearing, replacing former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan
In the same omnibus motion, the Ombudsman also asked the court to allow Guevarra to remain in the custody of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
Guevarra surrendered to the NBI on Nov. 19.

Clavano said Guevarra's testimony could prove crucial to the case because, as a foreign exchange firm executive, he may provide insight into how large-scale corruption proceeds are handled in cash, often leaving little documentary or financial trail in the banking system.

“Pag ganito na kalaki 'yung nangyayaring korapsyon, usually hindi talaga dumadaan sa bangko 'yan," Clavano said during the Ombudsman's weekly radio program, TanodBayan, aired over state-run Radyo Pilipinas.
(When corruption reaches this magnitude, transactions usually do not go through banks.)
"Walang deposit slip, walang pirma, walang AMLC record na may nag-transfer ng funds from account A to account B. Usually diyan, cash na ang transactions nila,” he added.
(There are no deposit slips, signatures or Anti-Money Laundering Council records showing transfers between accounts. These transactions are usually conducted in cash.)
Guevarra could help investigators establish how cash was handled and moved, Clavano said.
He also suggested that the use of cash explained why investigators found little documentary evidence in financial records.
“Alam na ng mga public officials na hindi talaga dapat sila gumamit ng bangko kasi mahuhuli ka agad. That's all recorded. May paper trail 'yan, may pirma pa," Clavano said.
(Public officials already know they should not use banks because transactions are immediately recorded, leaving a paper trail and signatures.)
"So itong pagsuko ng isang foreign exchange [firm official], it will be substantial [to our case],” he added.
(That is why the surrender of a foreign exchange firm official would be substantial to the case.)

Clavano did not identify the transactions or individuals involved. However, the prosecution's AMLC financial investigator, Atty. Jan Mark Busa, had earlier told the Sandiganbayan that remittances worth P560.5 million to accounts linked to Romualdez from 2022 to 2025 were not related to flood control projects.
Clavano stressed that the Ombudsman had never claimed that the alleged proceeds of corruption were transferred directly to Romualdez through bank accounts reflected in AMLC records.

“Wala naman talagang dadaan sa account. Hindi naman talaga 'yan ang theory ng Ombudsman. Ngayon, sumuko na 'yung sa money exchange [firm executive], dito natin malalaman kung ano talaga ang nangyari,” he said.

(Those transactions would not actually pass through bank accounts. That has never been the Ombudsman's theory. Now that the money exchange firm executive has surrendered, this is where we will find out what really happened.)

Meanwhile, Romualdez's lawyer, Judd Roy III, questioned the prosecution's move to replace Bonoan as a witness, saying the defense had prepared its strategy based on the original set of prosecution witnesses and the criminal information filed against his client.

“The lines of defense were prepared, evidentiary positions were taken… even our cross-examination of the other witnesses was all in recognition of that [criminal] information [filed]. And now they're saying that it will not substantially affect the case," Roy said in a separate interview.
"Put yourself in our shoes. Do you honestly believe that is the case?” he added.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
articles.summary: A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

image.caption: The exhibition 'The Night Watch Lives' shows which microorganisms were found on the famous Rembrandt paintingImage: Noemi Achthoven/ARTIS

blocks.text: Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.
Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?
The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

blocks.caption: 'The Night Watch Lives' study is conducted in collaboration with a major restoration and research project called 'Operation Night Watch'Image: Niels de Vries/Artis/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Putting microbes in the spotlight

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."
Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.
These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.
A study in progress

At the opening of the exhibition on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the upcoming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.
That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

blocks.caption: Microbiologist Eline van Bloois will be taking samples from the original painting once a month, over a period of six monthsImage: Niels de Vries/ARTIS

blocks.text: People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."
The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.
As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.
When art and science meet

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch'."
The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.
And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."
The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.
