articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] ‘Be very, very afraid’
articles.summary: This year's Social Good Summit brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of…

blocks.text: We humans spent the last few days dissecting what’s been keeping us listless these days — artificial intelligence and the future of news.

Renowned historian and philosopher Yuval Harari warned us to be “very, very afraid” at this period in history. “AI is not a tool, it is an agent. It is something that can make decisions by itself. So it is taking power away from us,” he said.

But nothing is inevitable, Harari told Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa in a pre-recorded fireside chat that aired on Saturday, November 21, at Rappler’s annual Social Good Summit (SGS) at Shangri-La The Fort in Taguig. “There are still choices to be made.”

With the theme, “We, The Humans: Reclaim our Future,” this year’s SGS brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of no return.

items: We’re in a “new imperial age,” Harari said, warning the Philippines that it risks losing control of critical infrastructure because of its dependence on foreign technology. Read more.

Staunch human rights advocate Agnès Callamard, secretary-general of Amnesty International, pushed for collective resistance to Big Tech’s unfettered and opaque inroads into our personal and professional lives. To do that and to fight back, humans must first understand AI, Ressa said.

Singaporean economist and AI executive Leslie Teo outlined ways to develop AI as a positive force for society. Read more. (We will be publishing more stories and videos from the summit in the coming days. Watch out for them.)

blocks.text: AI was also raised as a “growing concern” by the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which held its 49th Summit in Manila last week. But whether the region intends to address it collectively is unclear.

In fact, the ASEAN Summit itself still failed to resolve critical regional issues that have been pending at the leaders’ desks: the civil war in Myanmar and the protracted negotiations for a South China Sea Code of Conduct. Read more.

In Turkey, the Antalya AI Pledge was launched on the sidelines of the COP 31 climate talks. It calls on governments and companies to take voluntary measures to power AI with cleaner energy. But China’s Alibaba is the only big tech company that has so far signed off on it.
Worse, the climate talks collapsed on Sunday, November 22, after leaders from the European Union and other countries rejected the final draft of a declaration that some deemed unambitious.

items: The draft acknowledged — for the first time — that global warming was on course to exceed the 1.5°C that countries had vowed to preserve. Read more.
The draft deal published on Thursday, November 19, removed any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels, prompting negotiators to extend their meetings to Sunday.
The first draft of the deal had already signaled tough negotiations ahead.

They got backups from ghosts — as the defense panel showed archived videos of the late senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and the late chief justice Renato Corona, who was convicted by the Senate impeachment court in 2013.

(I’m not sure that an English translation would do justice to that phrase.)

articles.title: Spying on survivors: Why RCMP watched Wab Kinew's father in the 1960s
articles.summary: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew wants to know who spied on his father for the RCMP, and why. Documents obtained by CBC News reveal the late Anishinaabe leader Tobasonakwut Kinew was under surveillance in…

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew holds an RCMP Security Service report about his late father from the 1960s contained in an intelligence dossier compiled on the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood, forerunner of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs. (Randall McKenzie/CBC News)

blocks.text: Inside the Manitoba premier's office, Wab Kinew unravels a state secret.

With a mix of wry amusement and serious concern, he flips through censored copies of the RCMP's historic surveillance dossiers, each one marked in pen as "racial intelligence," compiled on Indigenous organizations from the 1960s to the 1980s.

What he learns he calls damning and alarming: the Canadian government spied on his father, the late Anishinaabe leader Tobasonakwut Kinew, in a countrywide infiltration initiative later dubbed the "Native extremism program."

"Finding out that there was surveillance by law enforcement, by national security, for what today we would consider very routine political organizing and activism, it shows you, I would say, the racism of the time," the premier told CBC News in October.

At home in Orillia, Ont., Wab Kinew's uncle Fred Kelly untangles the same tale of espionage and deceit. He too was spied on for lawful democratic activism in the '60s, though it's hardly a surprise. He strongly suspected it.

"I had no actual proof that I was being spied upon, but I knew it," said Kelly, also known as Kiizhebowse Makwa, a distinguished Anishinaabe elder, spiritual leader and former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3 in northwestern Ontario.
Anishinaabe elder gets proof of long-suspected RCMP spying

CBC News provided these documents to the family for the first time during a years-long investigation into Canada's Cold War-era program to spy on Indigenous leaders and activists, which the RCMP created and which CSIS revived in the late 1980s.

The story of this one famous family reveals how many RCMP surveillance targets were residential school survivors who went on to lead legitimate political movements to reclaim their identity. To them, it's no shock the government that openly suppressed First Nations culture in residential schools also tried to suppress their newfound political voice.
As former national chief Georges Erasmus put it in an interview earlier this year, "It is just the next chapter of oppression."
From residential school to resistance
Tobasonakwut Kinew was about seven years old when he was taken to St. Mary’s Indian Residential School in Kenora in northwestern Ontario in the 1940s, where he experienced almost a decade of horrors.

Catholic priests and nuns tried to strip him of his culture by cutting his hair short, changing his name from Tobasonakwut to Peter Kelly and giving him a number, 54. He suffered psychological, physical and sexual abuse.
Eight-year-old Tobasonakwut standing with his grandfather, Kaagagewannakweb, who came to visit him at St Mary's Residential School in Kenora, Ont., circa 1944-45. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)
Both as a CBC reporter and in his 2015 memoir, Wab Kinew candidly explored his father's residential school experience and how the resulting trauma nearly severed the ties that bind a family together.

"Look at my dad, he had the Indian agent deciding everything about his life in his early years, until he went to residential school when it was a boys' keeper and a priest … Then he left and it was back to the Indian Agent. And then this surveillance," Wab Kinew told CBC News.

"There's a longer history of government and corporate entities monitoring Indigenous families, assigning numbers, assigning qualitative evaluations of them, but seemingly not engaging with them as people."
Fred Kelly's experience was similar. He said he suffered physical and sexual abuse as well, and he too got the Irish surname Kelly at St. Mary’s, where he was taken at five years old.
"My impression of the residential school system was very much a system of incarceration to teach me and to force me to believe that my system, my original system of spirituality, was wrong," he said.
Fred Kelly (left) and Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) in their 20s in an undated photo taken in their community, Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)

The 6,000 pages of formerly secret intelligence files gathered on First Nations leaders by the RCMP Security Service and obtained by CBC News under access to information law reveal another chapter in this story.

As the brothers joined a generation of Indigenous leaders getting organized politically, it was no longer priests and nuns giving them numbers but Mounties — giving them file numbers as perceived subversives.
Fred Kelly entered the national political spotlight in November 1965, when he organized a pivotal protest in Kenora against racial injustice, now hailed as the country's first civil rights march.
Newspapers called Kenora Canada's Alabama and compared the racial tensions to "Bloody Sunday" in Selma, where Alabama state troopers attacked peaceful Black civil rights marchers earlier in 1965.
"Our people did not do these kinds of things. Our people are rather stoic: If that's the way it is, that's what we've got to live with," Kelly recalled.
Indigenous people demand a better deal in Kenora, Ont. in 1965

Town council mocked him, saying he'd be lucky if four people showed up. Instead between 400 and 500 Anishinaabeg filled Kenora's streets, marching in a silent and peaceful but proud show of dignity that still inspires First Nations leaders 60 years later.
"We were not looking for love," Kelly said.
"We were looking for justice and equality."
'Known agitators'
The premier's father and uncle, or the "Kelly brothers," soon gained celebrity and notoriety.

The Globe and Mail ran the headline "Indian brothers predict Kenora race riots" after a group of white men attacked them in 1967, and CBC flew them to Toronto to discuss the incident on national television.

The RCMP Security Service, a domestic intelligence agency that became CSIS in 1984, took notice, too. Amid the paranoia of the Cold War, Mounties feared radicals and communists could infiltrate and exploit the First Nations rights movement.
By 1969, Mounties had Winnipeg-based human sources informing on the brothers. One informer meticulously tracked Fred Kelly's movements and politics, depicting him as a potentially violent subversive.
"The source considers him to be a radical and somewhat dangerous person," an intelligence investigator reported.

In a separate report, a Mountie in Winnipeg reported both brothers "have been connected with the 'Red Power' movement." The RCMP labelled them as "known agitators" and tracked their movements across Canada.

Fred Kelly is unsurprised, but he still denounces these reports as "the wrong interpretation of what I was seeking." He draws parallels between how residential school officials carried out their mission and how Mounties did theirs.
"That was probably an order. How they carried that out is something that they have to live with," he said.
"But they did it in much the same way as those Catholic priests believed in what they were doing."
Diane Kelly, Wab Kinew's sister, was stunned and disappointed to see these references to her father and uncle.
"These are the things that we've always suspected, not just as a family, but as Indigenous people," said Diane Kelly, a former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3.
Diane Kelly says it's shocking and disappointing but not really surprising to see the contents of the declassified surveillance files. (Brett Forester/CBC)
In the 1970s, her father was helping bring back that grand council, laying the foundation for the resurgence of the very political body she later led, she said.
"How was that terrorism? How was that being an agitator? It's about having pride in who you are and knowing who you are," she said.

By 1971, the Security Service explicitly targeted the legitimate Indigenous movement, writing in a secret, urgent-marked report that "the activities of the National Indian Brotherhood," now the Assembly of First Nations, were "of special interest to us."

"As stressed in previous correspondence forwarded to all divisions, the organized activity of our Canadian Indians are of interest," the report said, calling it "most desirable" if the brotherhood's annual spring conference was infiltrated with "human source coverage."
Singled out as top targets were Fred Kelly and Tobasonakwut Kinew, or Peter Kelly. Their movement, in other words, was compromised.
Jeffrey Copenace, chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, where the brothers and premier are from, is outraged.

Chief of the Ojibways of Onigaming Jeff Copenace speaks to reporters following the First Nations Summit at the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Que., in July 2025. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)
"These two men should be celebrated along with all of the other Treaty 3 and First Nation leaders that have been trying to attain human rights in Canada," he said.

"To think that these two men had their privacy infiltrated, that there's all kinds of documentation about them that they're not aware of that's just coming to light now, it's a bit sad. It's just a little bit heartbreaking."

In response to the rise of the American Indian Movement and arrival of Red Power activism, the RCMP Security Service intensified the surveillance and expanded the dragnet by formally establishing a full-time "Red Power desk" in Ottawa in 1973.

items: Why Mounties paid 5 informers to spy on Dene leaders: Inside a secret surveillance operation
How RCMP spies infiltrated the 1970s Indigenous rights movement

blocks.text: Here, intelligence officers tapped phones and paid informers to infiltrate groups like the National Indian Brotherhood and Dene Nation. The RCMP files name 150 Mounties involved, dozens of organizations monitored, and hundreds of individuals targeted.
"When you hear these actions, it's hard to believe that reconciliation is really a tangible thing in Canada," said Copenace.
What now?
At the Manitoba legislature, Wab Kinew has questions. First, naturally, is "who were these informants?" But that evolves into a call for all-around clarity.
"Was the RCMP paying people? Were people giving this information under duress?" he said.
"Does the way that this information enters the permanent record speak to whether it is credible or not? Were people being induced? Bribed?"

Using informers to infiltrate legitimate movements is far from harmless, said John Carlson, who is Anishinaabe from Red Rock Indian Band in northwestern Ontario and an associate professor of criminology at the University of Ottawa. He argues this countersubversion program had a chilling effect on political activism and free expression.
Associate professor John Carlson teaches his students at the University of Ottawa about the significance of the silent march in Kenora led by Fred Kelly in 1965. (Brett Forester/CBC News)
"That's the legacy. It's purging the movement of what the RCMP, I'm sure, would call subversive ideology and organizational practices," Carlson said.
"But I would call [those practices] relevant to fighting for a society where Indigenous dignity, self-determination and relations, responsibilities and values could also shape this society."
Ultimately Tobasonakwut Kinew and Fred Kelly became political and community leaders, leaving an indelible mark on Canadian history.

Fred Kelly was part of the team that negotiated the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement that led to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Tobasonakwut Kinew personally reconciled with Pope Benedict in 2009, presenting him with an eagle feather and ceremonial pipe. Both brothers were on Parliament Hill in 2008 to witness prime minister Stephen Harper's historic apology for the residential school system.

Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) holds the Assembly of First Nations ceremonial staff on his way to a news conference after Pope Benedict's general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, April 29, 2009. (Pier Paolo Cito/The Associated Press)

As for the spying, RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme issued a statement of regret after CBC News revealed the program's existence in May 2026, but the Assembly of First Nations continues to seek a full apology, access to uncensored files and answers.
Public Safety Minister Gary's Anandasangaree office said in September that he is working with relevant federal departments to support the release of those documents.

For Wab Kinew, the files confirm Canada's intelligence service of the 1960s "was racist," but he believes those organizations today have a more progressive and egalitarian view. On that front, Manitoba's first Anishinaabe premier finds a silver lining in his relationship with the RCMP today.
Mounties still follow him around the country, as they did his father. It's just no longer the secret spy branch. It's the executive protection unit.

articles.title: DA plans P18B budget for agri mechanization in 2027 to boost production
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it is eyeing up to P18 billion in the 2027 budget for agricultural machinery.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 5:57pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it is eyeing up to P18 billion in the 2027 budget for agricultural machinery.

Most of the government’s budget for mechanization is under the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF), including the P9 billion allotted for rice machinery. But the DA is seeking a bigger allocation for farm machinery for other crops.

“But of course, the Department of Agriculture through its other programs also have machineries. I would safely assume we can easily almost double that,” said DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. in a press briefing during the Asia Pacific Conference on Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization.
“So we might have about P15 to 18 billion for 2027 available for farm machinery and motor vehicles,” he added.
The Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and Mechanization (PhilMech) said that an additional P50 billion is needed to fully mechanize the rice sector alone.
“In the span of six years, we only mechanized around 60 % to 70% of our rice. So we're still needing 30% more,” said PhilMech director Dionisio Alvindia in the press briefing.
“That could value around P50 billion more to mechanize the whole system,” he added.

The Philippine government is pushing for accessible and sustainable mechanization of the agriculture sector to boost production, without leaving small farmers behind despite the modernization efforts.

“Modernization must be practical, accessible, and responsive to the realities of our farmers. It requires appropriate technologies, affordable financing, supportive policies, reliable after-sales services, and just as importantly, the skills to operate and maintain these machineries,” said Tiu Laurel Jr.
Meanwhile, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) noted that farmers will only invest in technologies that will boost their income.

“Farmers are some of the most innovative, risk-taking individuals that you will ever meet. But when we think about the evolution of technology and adoption of it, a farmer will not invest in a new technology unless she knows that it saves her money or helps her make a profit,” said FAO Deputy Director General Beth Bechdol in the press briefing.
However, the DA assured that mechanization of the agriculture sector won’t mean replacing farmers or any other human force in the sector.
“Machines should make farmers more productive, not make farmers irrelevant,” said Tiu Laurel Jr. —LDF, GMA News

articles.summary: Anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt had asked the Senate ethics panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine if he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose…

blocks.text: BATO. Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa speaks to members of the media, at the Senate on May 13, 2026.
Rappler

Anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt had asked the Senate ethics panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine if he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose appropriate sanctions if warranted

items: Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa has requested the Senate ethics committee to dismiss a complaint regarding his prolonged absence from the Senate, arguing that it lacks sufficient grounds.
The complaint was filed by the anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt, which sought an investigation into Dela Rosa's absence and potential violations of Senate rules.
Dela Rosa is also involved in a legal battle concerning an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court related to his role in the anti-drug campaign during the Duterte administration.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa has asked the Senate ethics committee to dismiss a complaint against him over his prolonged absence from the Senate.

In a response submitted to the Senate committee on ethics and privileges, Dela Rosa, through his legal counsel Israelito Torreon, sought the dismissal of a complaint filed by anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt in February.
The group had asked the Senate panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine whether he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose appropriate sanctions if warranted.

In a notice, the Senate ethics panel informed dela Rosa that they had found the complaint to be compliant with requirements “both in form and in substance” following an executive session on October 22. The panel directed Dela Rosa to submit a written response within 15 days of receiving the notice.
Dela Rosa’s office confirmed receiving the notice on November 19.
In his response, Torreon argued that the complaint should be dismissed for “insufficiency in form and substance, and for failure to state any offense cognizable by the Committee.”

Dela Rosa also asked the committee to hold the proceedings in abeyance pending the resolution of his camp’s motion for reconsideration of the Supreme Court ruling that denied his plea for a temporary restraining order (TRO) against the enforcement of the International Criminal Court warrant.
He also asked the committee to deny the motion included in the complaint, seeking the suspension of his Senate office’s operations, including the release of salaries and operational expenses.

“In the event the Committee proceeds further, furnish respondent with copies of all records on which it intends to rely, and afford him a hearing, through counsel, with the opportunity to examine the complainants and their witnesses and to present evidence,” he added.
Senate ethics committee chairperson Vicente “Tito” Sotto III confirmed receiving Dela Rosa’s response.

“I received the answer via email on Saturday, November 21, 2026, 8:51 pm. It was submitted through his counsel and not signed by him personally. This answer will be considered in the next Ethics hearing that will be scheduled at the soonest time,” Sotto told reporters in a Viber message.
In October, Dela Rosa again asked the SC to reverse its earlier ruling denying his plea for a TRO against the enforcement of the ICC arrest warrant.
Dela Rosa is among the former officials of the Rodrigo Duterte administration implicated in the bloody anti-drug campaign, which human rights organizations say resulted in nearly 30,000 deaths.

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued an arrest warrant against the senator in November 2025 over his alleged role in the drug war. The court identified him as a co-perpetrator in the case, saying those involved “controlled a structure of power” that enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out the killings.
The warrant remained under seal until May 11 of this year, when it was made public.

Dela Rosa had been absent from the Senate for months before appearing on May 11 to support Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s bid for the Senate presidency. He then remained inside the Senate building for three days as he sought refuge from possible arrest.

A shooting incident erupted on the night of May 13, allegedly triggered by Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Mao Aplasca, Dela Rosa’s Philippine Military Academy classmate. Hours later, at around 2:30 am, Dela Rosa left the Senate building, accompanied by his political ally, Senator Robin Padilla.
Dela Rosa has since stayed out of public view.
In seeking a reconsideration of the SC ruling, Dela Rosa’s lawyer argued that the enforcement posture against the senator had “escalated” while the motion remained unresolved.

The motion also cited developments since the original petition, including the Department of the Interior and Local Government’s declaration of Dela Rosa as “armed and dangerous” and the P50-million bounty offered for his arrest. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine was behind attack on Russian warship off Libya
articles.summary: Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a naval base in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the vessel in a surprise assault the…

blocks.text: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine carried out drone attacks on Russian vessels off Libya

Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a naval base in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian corvette Merkury, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbour, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."
Russian officials made no immediate comment.

Within Ukraine, a Russian strike on a five-storey apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A seven-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.
A rescue worker climbs a ladder to a balcony of a residential building damaged in a Russian strike in Kyiv on Monday. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)

Federico Borsari, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told CBC News that while it isn't "completely novel" for Ukraine to deploy drones away from the main theatre of war — pointing to the skirmishes in the Black Sea — the Ukrainian attack off the North African coast demonstrates more than others before it that "there is no safe haven for Russian assets."

"I think the real key element here is that Ukraine has been able to deploy not just drones from ships or from secure locations near the areas where Russian assets are located, but also to deploy constant, near-real-time surveillance, reconnaissance, intelligence capabilities," he said.

David Hambling, a London, U.K.-based journalist and author who writes about war and military technology, said the attack carries wider implications for the use of drones in warfare. While the Houthis and Iranians have used unmanned sea vehicles for drone attacks in the Middle East, he said, the capabilities demonstrated by Ukraine in the near-five-year war with Russia are of a different magnitude.

If Ukraine can achieve this kind of attack, Hambling said, "that means the Iranians, the North Koreans, the Chinese, the Russians — anyone can potentially use the same technique to attack any ship anywhere and then deny responsibility."
Ukraine hails 'unique' attack
The operation — conducted near Benghazi, some 2,400 kilometres from the front line in Ukraine — was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit more than 40 aircraft parked near airbases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometre front line snaking through southern and Eastern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.

In satellite images provided by Vantor, a vessel is seen at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, before and after being struck. Ukraine claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it sank the Russian warship Merkury. (Vantor/CBC)

Ukraine has also hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and other Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address on Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.
On Sunday, Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara near Benghazi, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter, he said.

Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.
The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.
A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.
Russian defences tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.

items: With Putin in the room, Carney condemns Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine
Trump calling Putin a friend is 'appalling,' says former ambassador to NATO

blocks.text: Reuters verified the Angara and Merkury attack through satellite imagery and handout photos from the Libyan National Army, comparing the ships' superstructures, shapes and colours, as well as the position of nearby cranes.

The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres and the UN Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.
Several injured, Libyan officials say

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, and used the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an airbase in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.
A Ukrainian drone approaches the Russian cargo ship MV Angara near Benghazi, Libya, in video provided by the Security Service of Ukraine on Monday. (Security Service of Ukraine/The Associated Press)

Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a co-operation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.

articles.title: COP flop triggers backlash in Australia; Pacific nations express despair
articles.summary: 'We have been let down on all sides,' the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 says in a statement

blocks.text: Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of COP31 Negotiations Chris Bowen speaks to members of the media at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, November 22, 2026. REUTERS/Murad Sezer
Murad Sezer/Reuters
'We have been let down on all sides,' the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 says in a statement

items: The COP31 climate talks in Turkey failed to reach a final agreement, leading to calls for the resignation of Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who faced criticism for the outcome.

The conference, attended by over 190 countries, was marked by contention over fossil fuel discussions, with significant pressure from oil-producing nations like Saudi Arabia, resulting in a lack of collective action on climate change.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The finger-pointing to assign blame for the collapse of UN climate talks in Turkey began on Monday, November 23, with calls for the resignation of the Australian minister leading them, while the Pacific island nations most at risk expressed their despair over the failure of countries to collectively address global warming.

For the first time since the 2009 meeting in Copenhagen, the COP climate conference could not reach a final agreement from its talks after the EU and others rejected a final deal that did not include any mention of fossil fuels’ role in global warming because of pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing nations.

This was the first meeting since the UN’s environmental body confirmed global temperatures were set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) level scientists have said will cause extreme weather impacts to intensify, and the lack of collective action has increased a sense of impotence around the multilateral COP process.

Turkey hosted the latest talks, called COP31, in Antalya but shared leadership with Australia. Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen was the COP31 president of negotiations, and opposition politicians in his home country blamed him for the failure.
“This energy minister’s got to go because he’s a complete and utter failure,” Angus Taylor, a member of the Australian parliament who leads the opposition, told reporters on Monday.
“Chris Bowen was responsible for it. He should go,” Taylor said.
Speaking after the COP31 talks, Bowen blamed the very strong red lines many parties had on climate change.

Inside the Australian parliament, other opposition members asked Prime Minister Anthony Albanese why he would not sack Bowen after the country had spent A$150 million ($99.23 million) on COP31. Albanese did not comment directly on whether he would ask Bowen to step down.
“We believe that climate change is real. We believe in the science,” Albanese said. “Whether it’s environmental security or national security, we act in Australia’s national interest.”

The COP31 talks began on November 9, but the lack of a final agreement extended the summit to a record overtime on Sunday, November 22. There was already some contention before their start as Australia, which has been at the forefront of efforts to act against global warming, fought with Turkey over hosting duties.
More than 190 countries were represented, and more than 92,000 people had registered, making it provisionally the largest UN climate conference on record. The United States did not send a delegation.
Last year’s talks in Belém, Brazil, produced a deal but no commitment to phase out fossil fuels.

China is the world’s biggest emitter of carbon dioxide, the main cause of global warming, and a spokesman for the country’s foreign ministry, Guo Jiakun, expressed disappointment at the COP31 outcome during a news conference on Monday but said it “should not lead to a loss of confidence in multilateral process.”
Guo added that addressing climate change is a “shared undertaking for humanity” and the global trend toward low-carbon development is “irreversible.”
Bhupender Yadav, who led India’s delegation at COP31, said India engaged constructively and tirelessly with the presidencies and other parties.
“While concerns remain over certain elements of the cover decision, we remain committed to dialogue and constructive engagement until the very end to build consensus,” he said.
Most Pacific island nations, which are facing rising sea levels and other existential threats from climate change, expressed deep disappointment.
“We have been let down on all sides,” the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 said in a statement.

Tuvalu, the Pacific island nation that hosted a pre-COP event in October highlighting its exposure to rising sea levels, called out the absence of engagement and transparency in trying to reach a decision on a final statement.

“Listening to parties who diminish the credibility of signs of climate change is disappointing,” said Maina Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, expressing concern about the lack of commitment to put the world back on track for the global temperature goal. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duterte’s drug war is state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission
articles.summary: 'Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value,' says Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan

blocks.text: DRUG WAR. Relatives of war on drugs victims take part in a candle-lit vigil to commemorate the 10th anniversary of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s anti-drug campaign at the Bantayog ng Bayani in Quezon City on July 1, 2026.
'Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value,' says Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan

MANILA, Philippines – A week before former president Rodrigo Duterte’s historic trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30, a local truth commission released its initial report on his war on drugs.

The Philippine Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Truth Commission) said on Monday, November 23, that the so-called drug war was systemic and inflicted by Duterte’s government on thousands of victims.

“Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value. In the cases families brought to us, no one has been held to account,” said Truth Commission chairperson and former ICC judge Raul Pangalangan.

“When killings jump in the weeks after a president tells police he will protect them if they kill, when they fall almost to nothing each time the police are pulled out of the campaign, and when they continue through Christmas and All SoulsDay, the pattern points away from chance and toward policy,” the commission said in its report.
Duterte’s campaign promise in 2016 was to eliminate illegal drugs and criminality.
After he was sworn in as the 16th president in July, he immediately launched his drug war led by the Philippine National Police (PNP) and now fellow ICC co-accused, Senator Bato dela Rosa.
On his first day as president on July 1, 2016, Duterte told the PNP that even if they killed a thousand people in line of their duty, he will protect them.

blocks.caption: Duterte to PNP: ‘Do your duty and I will die for you’

blocks.text: Launched in May, the Truth Commission seeks to provide credible documentation of the killings linked to Duterte’s drug war. It held truth-telling sessions with the victims’ families to humanize drug war victims, analyze evidence, and demand accountability and reforms. Some of the findings came from these sessions, as well as from other sources.
On Monday, the commission said there were 8,230 people killed in the drug war, based on its initial count. This number is much higher compared to the government’s count.

“The governments most cited figure, 6,252, covers only deaths in police and PDEA (Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency) operations. The 12,000 to 30,000 range cited by the ICC Prosecutor draws on several published estimates. These figures count different things; no consensus exists on the number of the dead,” the commission explained.
Apart from the initial count, the commission also released the following key findings:

items: 96.6% of the victims were men in their working and parenting years.
More than half or 56% of the killings were in Metro Manila and Central Luzon
Killings fell when police were pulled out from drug war operations.
24 of 46 exhumed victims had been shot in the head, while many killings bear the marks of execution.
People arrested during the drug war campaign remain in congested jails and prisons.

blocks.caption: Duterte’s drug war is state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission

blocks.text: The Truth Commission said its initial report will be available to everyone, including the Philippine government. Pangalangan said these findings will be shared to anyone who will find it useful, even national and international government and nongovernmental organizations.
Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, who served as one of the reactors during the Truth Commission’s event, said they will look into the findings once transferred to the Department of Justice.

“These administrative investigations…. These are these are technically not final and definitive, right? As the pieces of evidence come along or made available, right? You adjust based on what’s…the truth and what’s available,” Vida said in a mix of Filipino and English.

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, since March 2025 after he was arrested due to crimes against humanity. His case stemmed from his drug war and the killings allegedly committed by the Davao Death Squad.
On November 30, the former president will be the first Asian head of state to face a trial due to crimes against humanity before the ICC. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
articles.summary: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension…

image.caption: Germany's aging population and low birth rate mean fewer young people are entering the workforceImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.
In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.

As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.
To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.

Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.
How does the Early Start Pension work?
Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager between the ages of six and 18.

Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.
Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.
Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.
Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.

"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.
"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said.
The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.
It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens."
What does the government say?

The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.
Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.
Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.
But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.
The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.
What Germans young and old think about the pension system
Can the scheme encourage long-term investing?

Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.

"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them."
Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.
"If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions."
In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.

Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.

Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.
"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he said.
What else should be done to stabilize the pension system?
Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.
Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, says the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.

"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.

The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to give update to MPs after ‘landmark’ UK-EU summit – UK politics live
articles.summary:
PM expected to tell Commons that Friday’s deal will be ‘the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament’

Good morning. This afternoon Andy Burnham will…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 14m agoAndy Burnham to give update to MPs after ‘landmark’ UK-EU summit

blocks.text: Andy Burnham to give update to MPs after ‘landmark’ UK-EU summit

Good morning. This afternoon Andy Burnham will make a statement to MPs about the UK-EU summit on Friday where agreements were reached on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. At one point there were suggestions that he might use this Commons moment to give a speech with further details of his plan for a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU, including possibly rejoin. Now, that won’t happen today; Burnham has decided to make that announcement part of his 10-year plan, which is being unveiled next month. But dozens of MPs will get the chance to put a question to Burnham, and so we will get a sense of what they feel about the prospect of revisiting the Brexit settlement.
According to the BBC, Burnham will describe the Friday deal as “the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament”.
He tell Parliament on Monday the “landmark” deal struck with the EU means there is a “very real prospect” the next decade can be “much better” than the last one.

We will hear alternative views at the CBI conference today. All the main UK opposition party leaders are speaking, and Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, are planning to criticise the agreement with Brussels, according to extracts of their remarks released overnight.

Burnham won’t be there himself. But he is sending his de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, and she is planning to reassure the CBI audience that Burnham’s plan for more public control of utilities does not mean the government is anti-business.
Haigh will say:

double quotation markThis government will put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology. Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.
She will point out that foreign governments already own “significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks with returns paid to their taxpayers” and she will say:
double quotation markThe status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.
In its overnight briefing on the speech, the Cabinet Office says:

double quotation markChallenging the misconception that public control means wholesale nationalisation, the first secretary will say this approach is not about whether or not markets work, but how effective monopolies have resulted in a lack of genuine competition.
Here is the agenda for the day.

9.30am: Rain Newton-Smith, the CBI chief executive, opens the annual CBI conference with a speech. There are also speeches from Lousie Haigh, the first secretary of state, at 9.45am and Kemi Badenoch at 12.20pm, and Q&A events with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, at 2.35pm, Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, at 3.55pm and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, at 4.40pm.
Morning: Andy Burnham is due to visit a Morrisons in Kent to promote claims his SPS deal with the EU will help keep down food prices.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Burnham is expected to make a statement to the Commons about Friday’s UK-EU summit.

blocks.text: Follow below for developments from the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday, November 23:
November 23, 2026
NATO to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace

Parallel to the continuing NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, representatives of the alliance's member states are also set to convene in Brussels on Monday to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.

Russian drones and missiles have frequently penetrated the sovereign airspace of Poland, a European Union and NATO member, in the course of air strikes against neighboring Ukraine over the past four years.
According to the Polish government, three Russian missiles entered Polish airspace on Friday, crashing in the south-east of the country.
Airspace violations have also been reported in other NATO and EU countries including Romania, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
On Saturday, Finland reported a suspected airspace violation by a manned Russian military helicopter near the southeastern town of Loviisa.
Moldova, which is not in the EU or NATO, has also reported airspace violations, most recently this weekend.

articles.title: Quebec MNAs must swear oath to the King, judge rules
articles.summary: A Quebec Superior Court judge has suspended the province’s law that made the mandatory oath to King Charles optional, ordering that members of the province's legislature must swear allegiance before…

image.caption: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon speaks at the National Assembly during the swearing-in ceremony of Parti Québécois (PQ) MNAs in October. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers will deliver his decision today on a lawyer's attempts to block the start of parliamentary work this week, after the province's MNAs unanimously renounced the Oath of Allegiance during last month's swearing-in ceremonies.
Lawyer claims members' refusal to take oath threatens National Assembly's legitimacy
A decision on one lawyer's effort to delay the start of next week's parliamentary session in Quebec — until MNAs take the Oath of Allegiance — will be made today.

Lawrence David, a constitutional lawyer and University of Ottawa professor, is asking Quebec's Superior Court to delay the beginning of parliamentary work, claiming that until all MNAs take the oath to the King, any laws they pass will be illegitimate.
David has filed a lawsuit and an emergency injuction to suspend Bill 4, a provincial law passed in 2022 that made taking the oath optional for members of the National Assembly.
MNAs elected in October's general election took an oath to the people of Quebec — instead of to the monarchy — at swearing-in ceremonies last month.

items: Renouncing oath to the King threatens National Assembly's legitimacy, lawyer argues

blocks.text: During the election campaign earlier this year, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Québécois leader and current Quebec premier, said that his government would defund the office of Quebec's lieutenant-governor.
The premier further promised to "abolish whatever monarchy exists in Quebec."
Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers is expected to deliver his decision on the injunction at a Montreal courthouse around 10 a.m.
The decision comes just over a week before the National Assembly is set to resume on Dec. 1.
The parliamentary session was initially supposed to begin on Nov. 17, before being pushed back twice — first to Nov. 24, then to the beginning of December.

articles.title: Petition calls for Canadian telcos to answer customer calls within 10 minutes
articles.summary: An Ontario man says Canadians are fed up with long waits for telecom customer service. He’s launched a petition urging the federal government to require telcos to connect customers with a human agent…

image.caption: Frank Brown and hundreds of other Canadians have signed a petition he started, calling on the government to make companies like Rogers, Bell and Telus answer the phone — with a human agent — within 10 minutes. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

blocks.text: Frank Brown spent almost an hour on hold with Rogers last June, while simultaneously trying to get help through the company's online chat.
The Aurora, Ont., man was trying to find out why a $25 charge had appeared on his mother's account, which he manages.
After more than 40 minutes, he says he gave up on the chat because it wasn't helping. He soon abandoned the call, too.
Two days later, he tried calling Rogers again. This time he couldn't even get into the queue. A recorded message told him the system was overloaded and too busy to take his call.
"It isn't customer service if you can't talk to anybody," Brown said.
"Access to a human representative should not be treated as an additional premium service."

items: Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

blocks.text: For the last few months, Brown's been on a mission to get the federal government to take the issue seriously, launching a petition urging Ottawa to force telecom providers to connect with a human agent within 10 minutes.
"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "We need to make sure consumers are protected."
This man started a petition to force telcos to answer customer calls within 10 minutes | Go Public
Brown isn't alone in his frustration.
Long wait times, dropped calls, unhelpful agents and automated systems have sent customers in circles — frustrations Go Public and CBC Marketplace have documented across the country.

items: Customers complain about long wait times, multiple calls to resolve issues with Rogers, Telus and Bell
Telecom complaints have shot up 17%, with billing issues the main gripe, says watchdog

blocks.text: Complaints to the Commission for Complaints for Telecom-television Services (CCTS) were up 79 per cent in 2025-2026 over the previous year — ranging from billing and contract disputes to cancellation issues — but the telecom mediator has no mandate to specifically address customer service complaints, such as long wait times. That leaves customers with no independent avenue to complain about the very service they're struggling to access.
And customer service has deteriorated dramatically, according to Mohammed Halabi, whose company MyBillsAreHigh.com helps businesses and individuals save money on telecom and internet costs.
"They've got to be held to account somehow," Halabi said. "The government has to do something."
Mohammed Halabi helps telco customers lower their bills. He says customer service has become 'absolutely horrible' over the last two years. (Michael Cole/CBC)
Go Public asked Rogers, Bell and Telus how they respond to calls for a mandatory 10-minute standard for answering customer calls.

Rogers declined an interview. A spokesperson sent a written statement saying the average wait time to reach a customer service representative was "around 7 minutes" this year — that figure does not include people on hold who give up after not getting through, like Brown. Rogers said a "very small percentage" of callers hang up before reaching a customer service rep and that the company is continuing to improve "the customer experience."
Telus and Bell both wrote that the "vast majority" of customer calls are answered within minutes.
Neither would specify what percentage of callers hang up after failing to reach a human agent — like Rogers, those customers are not included in their wait-time averages.
A growing chorus of complaints

After Brown filed a complaint with the CCTS, Rogers credited the $25 charge to his mother's account in July, calling it a "goodwill gesture." The company told Go Public it understood Brown had a "frustrating experience."

Since then, he's had to make several more calls to his telecom provider about other issues. Rogers says on average, Brown spent about four minutes getting routed to a customer service rep — but he says his concerns stand.
He initially launched a petition on Change.org, a petition platform, asking Canadians to support his call for better response times. So far, over 1,200 have signed.
Some have left comments describing two-hour waits, calling the delays "disgusting" and saying they felt "held hostage" on the phone.
Frank Brown spent nearly an hour on hold trying to resolve an issue with his mother's bill. (Submitted by Frank Brown)
Go Public has also received plenty of complaints from customers. Most emails are about Rogers, but some customers have also described difficulties getting through to Bell and Telus.
"It should not be this hard [to close an account]," wrote one person. "What in the world is going on with this company?"
"We have documented 18 separate call attempts totalling over 10.5 hours attempting to resolve this issue," wrote another.
"They keep laying people off, but cannot answer their phone," wrote another.
Customer service 'absolutely horrible'
Halabi says telecom customer service has become "absolutely horrible" over the last two years.

During that time, all three major telcos have laid off or offered buyouts to segments of their Canadian workforces. According to Unifor telecommunications director Roch LeBlanc, roughly 20,000 telecommunications jobs have been lost due to automation and offshoring in the last 10 to 15 years.
"It's just gotten so bad," Halabi said. "It's a constant circus."

items: CRTC to eliminate fees when cancelling or switching cellphone and internet plans

blocks.text: He also believes telecom companies are increasingly trying to push artificial intelligence over the use of human agents — technology that can frustrate customers when it misunderstands what callers are saying or directs them to the wrong department.
"All of this is creating a sense of anxiety, especially for senior citizens."
Spain's new 3-minute law

Before retiring two years ago, Brown spent eight years as president of a company that employed dozens of people. For years, he says, he personally responded to every consumer review because he wanted customers to know "the person at the top" cared about their business.

"I hate the hypocrisy of Rogers courting me on TV — as if me giving them my business is very much appreciated — and then hearing ‘your call is important to us' while waiting forever for them to answer the phone," he told Go Public.
Brown believes telecom companies should be held to a measurable customer-service standard, as is the case in Spain.

Spain passed legislation last December requiring companies with more than 250 employees to ensure that when customers request a human agent, they can reach one within three minutes in 95 per cent of cases.
"Three minutes is pretty aggressive," said Brown, which is why he thought a 10-minute standard would be a reasonable starting point here.
"It's the Canadian way, we're nice people."
Telecom complaints soar as Canadians rail over billing issues

Hoping to get action from the federal government, Brown also launched a parliamentary petition, which would compel a written response from the government should it reach 500 signatures by Nov. 26. As of Nov. 19, it was sitting at 425 signatures.

The petition calls on the federal government to direct the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to establish "clear, measurable and enforceable" customer service standards for telecommunications providers.

Specifically, it calls for a "maximum 10-minute telephone hold time" for customers seeking access to a human agent and requests "meaningful and proportional consequences" for providers that persistently fail to meet that standard.
"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "As long as we're going to limit competition in the industry, we need to make sure that us consumers are protected."

items: Rogers, Bell, Telus under fire for charging fees that 'appear' to violate new rules

blocks.text: Brown is also scheduled to discuss his petitions when he appears before the CRTC next week, as it begins hearings on protections for home phone, wireless, TV and internet consumers.
"There's a real feeling that we just have to accept [bad customer service]," he said. "And I decided, no, I'm going to try and do something about it."
Submit your story ideas
Go Public is an investigative news segment on CBC-TV, radio and the web.
We tell your stories, shed light on wrongdoing and hold the powers that be accountable.

If you have a story in the public interest, or if you're an insider with information, contact gopublic@cbc.ca with your name, contact information and a brief summary. All emails are confidential until you decide to Go Public.

articles.title: Inside India's bold plan to transform its largest slum, Dharavi, into a multibillion-dollar development
articles.summary: India's largest slum is being cleared to make room for a modern urban development to include rehabilitated slum housing plus luxury condos and office towers. It's a massive regeneration project,…

image.caption: An animation gif shows daily life in Dharavi, Mumbai, India's largest slum, where roughly a million people live in impoverished conditions. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

blocks.text: In a memorable flashback from the 2008 Oscar-winning film Slumdog Millionaire, brothers Jamal and Salim Malik sit atop an unfinished high-rise overlooking the Mumbai neighbourhood where they grew up. Their childhood slum has been bulldozed and replaced by luxury apartments and commercial skyscrapers.
"That used to be our slum. Can you believe that, huh?" Salim remarks. "Now, it's all business. India is at the centre of the world."

What was fiction on screen is now unfolding in reality. Frontend loaders have moved into parts of Dharavi, India’s largest slum and the second-largest in the world, and are looking to turn it into a billion-dollar development, launching one of Asia’s most ambitious urban redevelopment projects.

Shopkeeper Pooja Tiwari, 29, watches anxiously as the diggers encroach on her tiny shop. She’s eked out a meagre living here for 14 years, but her landlord announced she’d have to be out within a week.
"I am very scared because my income has depended on this shop for so many years," she said. "I don’t know what I’m going to do."
Pooja Tiwari loses her shop in the first demolitions of Mumbai's Dhavari slum. It's her only income and she's nervous about how she'll survive. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
'A better place to live'

Dharavi is home to an estimated one million people, sprawling across nearly 600 acres in the heart of Mumbai. From the air, it looks like a sea of thousands of bright blue tarps covering ramshackle, one- to three-storey structures.
At the heart of it is a dense rabbit warren of tiny rooms and lanes less than a metre wide, squished so tightly together that little sunlight reaches the ground, even at midday.
Households lack formal water and sewer systems, sharing communal taps and toilets, while tangled, outdated wiring supplies electricity.
Mumbai wants this slum gone. Where will 1 million people go?

Mahendra Kalyankar, CEO of the state's Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA), says that more than 1,000 people often share a single toilet, and 100 rely on one drinking water tap; the school dropout rate, he says, hovers around 40 per cent.
"New Dharavi will be a better place to live," he said, referring to the plans for modern tiny apartments in highrise buildings, with proper sanitation and hygiene.
State and city officials have tried for decades to uproot Dharavi. But this time a bold new plan is underway.

items: Countries vulnerable to climate disaster push for faster, easier access to finance at COP31

blocks.text: To transform the slum, the Maharashtra state government has partnered with the Adani Group, led by multi-billionaire Gautam Adani, in a public-private venture. Pranav Adani, the founder's nephew, described the conditions inside Dharavi as "inhuman," at a recent Mumbai conference, framing the project as building "a city in a city" and a huge opportunity.

Mahendra Kalyankar, CEO of the state Slum Rehabilitation Authority promises better living conditions for slum residents in Dharavi. With the Adani Group, the government is launching a big bold plan to build modern apartments alongside a glittering new residential and commercial centre in India's financial capital. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
Kalyankar says the difference this time is the injection of private capital, and the inclusion of the Adani Group, which can pay the substantial upfront costs.
"This project will be potentially successful when you infuse a lot of capital. That is the major issue," said Kalyankar.

It's valuable, because its sits on prime real estate next to the Bandra Kurla Complex, a landmark business district that houses banks, the stock exchange and multinational corporations. Local activists compare the 600-acre parcel to the Koh-i-Noor, the world-famous Indian diamond, just waiting to be claimed for a wealthy development.

"They are finding a big opportunity to extend this land to make BKC 2 and to make all the profit for one person [Adani] who is a big businessman of this city," said Samya Korde, a 26-year-old community organizer in Dharavi.
"Nobody dreams of living in choked lanes where sunlight doesn't come," she said. "So we want development to take place," but not by pushing residents out.
Many risk being pushed out

For over a year, surveyors have navigated Dharavi’s narrow alleys, measuring homes as small as 50 square feet and demanding paperwork to prove residency. Only families who can prove they lived in a street-level home there before 2000 are guaranteed a free apartment onsite.
Everyone else faces relocation: Some will be offered housing elsewhere, at a deep discount, while those who arrived more recently will be moved to rental units outside the area.

Samya Korde, 26, worries the plan to redevelop the Dharavi slum will mean a majority of its residents will be pushed out to other undesirable land, to make way for a wealthy urban neighbourhood. (Susan Ormiston/CBC)

Korde warns that 70 to 80 per cent of residents risk being labelled ineligible and pushed out to less desirable land. That figure is disputed, with the state government saying the surveys are incomplete. But critics and independent analysis argue that under the rules, a clear majority will not get new units on the same land.

She questions the development's motives: "There is one quote in Hindi: whether they want to remove poverty or whether they want to remove [the] poor," she said, "so that should be the aim — to transform people's lives and not to displace their homes."

items: What happens when a Google data centre comes to town? Southern India is finding out

blocks.text: To win over skeptics, the Adani Group recently opened an "Experience Centre" modelled after a luxury condo presentation facility. Visitors walk past murals celebrating Dharavi’s traditional artisans into a semi-circular theater playing a slick, IMAX-style promotional film.

The tour features a massive scale model of the future development — sleek commercial towers flanked by slum-rehabilitation high-rises — and a 350-square-foot show suite complete with a galley kitchen, a private toilet and two living spaces.

CBC News takes a tour of the Dharavi Experience Centre built by Adani to highlight the future look of the Dharavi Development. Luxury residences and office towers will be built alongside modern apartments for some slum residents. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
A lack of trust
For many residents, the glossy pitch masks a deep trust deficit.

Dharavi is an economic powerhouse. Generations of residents have built thriving, informal industries — leather tanneries, plastic recycling, commercial potteries — estimated to generate a billion dollars in annual turnover. Tradespeople remain skeptical of government promises that industrial operations can simply be moved into high-rise work zones serviced by freight elevators.

Meanwhile, an entrenched underground economy — including slum landlords profiting off unauthorized shanties and a local drug trade — is actively resisting a plan that allocates strictly one apartment per family.

For ordinary residents, the stakes are deeply personal. During a torrential downpour that threatened to flood the alleys and some of the homes, resident Khan Kabir Akhtar stood in a single-room home with his elderly grandfather, sitting on the bed.
Teenager Khan Kabir Akhtar and his grandfather both live in Dhavari. They want improvements, but in spite of harsh conditions, they don't want to move. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"My parents, my great-grandparents, [were] born here, so we want to live here," said Akhtar.

"We have to make it better, obviously," Akhtar admitted, but not at the cost of dislocating families. He doubts he will secure one of the new on-site apartments, and can't afford Mumbai market rates for another place to live.

items: 'It's like Groundhog Day': Waiting decades for justice in India's overburdened court system

blocks.text: Nearby, on what used to be railway lands, jackhammers are already pulverizing concrete and bulldozers are tearing into structures.

Down the lane, resident Rubina Sharif watches with cautious hope. Her modest home is slated for demolition, she’s waiting for interim housing before moving into a promised high-rise unit, given to qualifying slum residents.

"Redevelopment is a good plan," she said. "If it is genuinely meant to help the poor, then I am very happy about it. My expectation is simple: if we co-operate with them, they should also co-operate with us and not think only about themselves."

Rubina Sharif's home will be demolished. She welcomes improvements and is promised a new small apartment in Dharavi, but she worries about the developers making good on their commitments to the slum residents. (Saraskanth TK/CBC)

While the first new buildings could be ready within two years, the full transformation may take up to a decade. If successful, Mumbai’s massive urban experiment could serve as a blueprint for rapidly growing cities across Asia and Africa.

Yet in a city where affordable housing remains severely scarce and new slums can sprout within a month, erasing Dharavi will not solve Mumbai's housing crisis. While some families will finally trade squalor for modern living, hundreds of thousands of others face the prospect of being uprooted — and sequestered out of sight once again.
